nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-01.title: Prime factorization
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-01.body:
$2015=5\cdot13\cdot31$ is a product of three distinct primes. Three factors each greater than $1$ must each contain at least one prime, so they are exactly $5$, $13$, $31$ in some order, and $N+Y+C=49$.

**Answer: 49**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-02.title: Set up an equation
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-02.body:
Let there be $P$ pencils at $x$ cents each, and $28-P$ pens at $x+10$ cents. Then $Px+(28-P)(x+10)=300$, so $28x+280-10P=300$ and $28x=10P+20$. For $x$ to be a whole number of cents, $10P+20$ must be a multiple of $28$; with $P<20$ the only option is $P=12$ ($140=28\cdot5$). So a pencil costs $5$ cents.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-02.title: Count the pens
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-02.body:
Let there be $k$ pens. The cost is $28x+10k=300$, where $k=28-P>8$. So $300-10k$ must be a positive multiple of $28$ with $9\le k\le27$, i.e. one of $210,200,\dots,30$. Of these, only $140=28\cdot5$ is a multiple of $28$, at $k=16$. So a pencil costs $5$ cents (with $12$ pencils and $16$ pens: $60+240=300$).

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-03.title: Two equations
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-03.body:
Let Fiona be $x$ and Finn $y$ now. Then $x-10=2(y-10)+2$ and $x=1.5y$. Substituting: $1.5y-10=2y-18$, so $y=16$ and $x=24$.

**Answer: 24**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-04.title: Work rates
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-04.body:
Annie and Charlie together paint $\frac17+\frac18=\frac{15}{56}$ room per hour, so after one hour $\frac{41}{56}$ of the room remains. With Beth the rate is $\frac{15}{56}+\frac14=\frac{29}{56}$, so the rest takes $\frac{41}{56}\div\frac{29}{56}=\frac{41}{29}$ hours. Annie works the whole time: $1+\frac{41}{29}=\frac{70}{29}$ hours.

**Answer: $\frac{70}{29}$ hours**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-05.title: Factor
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-05.body:
$N^2-4N+3=(N-1)(N-3)$. For a positive prime, the factors have the same sign and one of them is $\pm1$. If $N-3=1$, then $N=4$ and the value is $3\cdot1=3$, prime. If $N-1=-1$, then $N=0$, not positive. Other options ($N-1=1$ gives $-1$; $N-3=-1$ gives $-1$) do not give primes. So $N=4$ is the only one.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-06.title: Form of the number
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-06.body:
A number with $6$ divisors has the form $p^5$ or $p^2q$ ($p,q$ distinct primes), since $6=6$ or $3\cdot2$. Odd $p^5$ is at least $3^5=243$, too big. For odd $p^2q$ below $100$: $9\cdot5=45$, $9\cdot7=63$, $9\cdot11=99$, $25\cdot3=75$ ($49\cdot3=147$ and $9\cdot13=117$ are too big).

**Answer: $45, 63, 75, 99$**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-07.title: Two per side
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-07.body:
A line meets a circle in at most $2$ points, so each of the $6$ sides meets the circle at most twice: at most $12$ points. This is achieved, e.g., by a regular hexagon and a concentric circle slightly smaller than its circumcircle (but larger than its incircle), which crosses every side twice.

**Answer: 12**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-08.title: Cases by repeated letters
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-08.body:
ADDITION has letters A, D, D, I, I, T, O, N: six different letters, with D and I available twice.
- Four different letters: $\binom64=15$.
- One pair (DD or II) plus two other different letters from the remaining $5$: $2\cdot\binom52=20$.
- Two pairs: $\{D,D,I,I\}$: $1$.

Total $15+20+1=36$.

**Answer: 36**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-09.title: Express the radius two ways
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-09.body:
$\pi r^2=4\pi x$ gives $r^2=4x$, and $2\pi r=6\pi x^2$ gives $r=3x^2$. Then $9x^4=4x$, and since $x\ne0$, $x^3=\frac49$.

**Answer: $\frac49$**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-10.title: Divisibility by 10, then 4
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-10.body:
The units digit of the sum is that of $A+A$, which must be $0$: $A=0$ or $A=5$.
- $A=5$: the sum is $\underline{B55}+\underline{BB5}=210B+60$; divisibility by $4$ needs $10B+60\equiv 2B\pmod 4$ to be $0$, so $B$ is even.
- $A=0$: the sum is $210B$, divisible by $4$ when $B$ is even.

$B$ is a nonzero digit (three-digit numbers), so $B\in\{2,4,6,8\}$ in both cases: $8$ ordered pairs.

**Answer: 8**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-10.title: Algebraic form
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-10.body:
$\underline{BAA}+\underline{BBA}=(100B+11A)+(110B+A)=210B+12A$. Mod $20$: $10B+12A\equiv0$. Mod $2$ this always holds; we need $5B+6A\equiv0\pmod{10}$. Mod $2$: $B$ even. Mod $5$: $6A\equiv A\equiv0$, so $A\in\{0,5\}$. With $B\in\{2,4,6,8\}$ that is $2\cdot4=8$ pairs.

**Answer: 8**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-11.title: Perfect cube
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-11.body:
With a single distinct root $a$ (of multiplicity $3$), the polynomial is $(x-a)^3=x^3-3ax^2+3a^2x-a^3$. Matching $-3a=-6$ gives $a=2$, and then $-a^3=-8$ checks. So $k=3a^2=12$.

**Answer: 12**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-12.title: Length of the tangent
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-12.body:
Join the centers (distance $R+r$) and drop a perpendicular from the smaller center to the radius of the larger circle at its tangent point. This makes a right triangle with legs $x$ and $R-r$ and hypotenuse $R+r$, so $x^2=(R+r)^2-(R-r)^2=4Rr=4N$ and $x=2\sqrt N$. This is an integer exactly when $N$ is a perfect square (if $4N=x^2$ then $x$ is even and $N=(x/2)^2$). The perfect squares $1,4,\dots,81$ give $9$ values (each is achieved with noncongruent circles, e.g. $R=2\sqrt N$, $r=\frac{\sqrt N}{2}$).

**Answer: 9**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-14.title: Distance from the center
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-14.body:
The line $5x-y+26=0$ is at distance $\frac{26}{\sqrt{25+1}}=\sqrt{26}$ from the origin. Since $\sqrt{26}>4$, the line misses the circle, and the shortest distance is $\sqrt{26}-4$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{26}-4$**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-14.title: Foot of the perpendicular
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-14.body:
The perpendicular from the origin is $y=-\frac15x$; it meets $y=5x+26$ where $-\frac x5=5x+26$, i.e. $x=-5$, at $(-5,1)$. That point is $\sqrt{26}$ from the origin, and the nearest point of the circle lies on the same ray, $4$ from the origin, so the distance is $\sqrt{26}-4$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{26}-4$**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-15.title: Isosceles triangle ABD
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-15.body:
Each interior angle of a regular octagon is $\frac{6\cdot180^\circ}{8}=135^\circ$. At $B$, $\angle ABD=135^\circ-60^\circ=75^\circ$. Since $BA=BC=BD$, triangle $ABD$ is isosceles, so $\angle BDA=\frac{180^\circ-75^\circ}{2}=52.5^\circ$. Then $\angle ADE=135^\circ-52.5^\circ=82.5^\circ=\frac{165}{2}^\circ$.

**Answer: $82.5^\circ$**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-16.title: Shift a negative solution
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-16.body:
$-8,-6,-4,-2$ satisfy all four conditions. Adding any multiple of $\operatorname{lcm}(8,6,4,2)=24$ keeps them, and the conditions are equivalent to $N\equiv-8\pmod{24}$ (since $8\mid N$ and $6\mid N+2$ force $N\equiv16\pmod{24}$, and then the other two hold). The least three-digit such $N$ is $16+4\cdot24=112$.

**Answer: 112**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-16.title: Check multiples of 8
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-16.body:
Three-digit multiples of $8$: $104$ fails because $106$ is not divisible by $6$. $112$: $114=6\cdot19$, $116=4\cdot29$, $118$ is even. So $N=112$.

**Answer: 112**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-17.title: Factor
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-17.body:
Adding $1$: $2xy+2x+y+1=24$, i.e. $(2x+1)(y+1)=24$. Here $2x+1$ is odd and at least $3$, and $y+1\ge2$. The odd divisors of $24$ are $1$ and $3$, so $2x+1=3$, $y+1=8$: the only pair is $(1,7)$.

**Answer: 1**

nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-18.title: Cut off three equilateral triangles
nyciml-2015-16-fall-sophfrosh-18.body:
Every interior angle of the hexagon is $120^\circ$, so the corner triangles $ADI$, $BEF$, $CGH$ have $60^\circ$ angles and are equilateral, with sides $AD=2$ and $BF=6$. On side $AC$: $AI+IH+HC=12$, so $HC=12-2-6=4$. Areas of equilateral triangles scale with the square of the side, so
$$\frac{[DEFGHI]}{[ABC]}=\frac{12^2-2^2-6^2-4^2}{12^2}=\frac{88}{144}=\frac{11}{18}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{11}{18}$**
